Four exercises at level 3, and every answer is graded on the number the formula returns.
Some totals need two columns multiplied before they are added, and some need to ignore rows a filter has hidden.

SUMPRODUCT multiplies arrays element by element and adds the results, which replaces a helper column. SUBTOTAL takes a function number first, so 9 adds and 1 averages, and it recalculates against the rows a filter leaves visible. AGGREGATE adds an options number that can ignore errors, hidden rows, or both. Choose the wrong option and the total is quietly wrong.

The two argument counts are what people mix up. A function number is a choice from a fixed list, an options number is a set of switches, and neither is a cell address. Write the pair down before building the formula. The group is short because each of these formulas is one argument away from a believable wrong answer.
A current version of Excel lets one formula return a block of cells, and this group uses that for three jobs.

The spill needs the room below it. Leave one row of data in the way and the whole result becomes an error rather than a short list. That is why the group checks where the answer lands and not only what it says. A spilled range holds no formula of its own, so typing over a cell inside it destroys the block.
Three exercises at level 3, all graded on the block a formula returns.

UNIQUE returns one copy of each distinct value in the order it met them, and an optional third argument keeps only values that appear once. FILTER returns the rows that meet a condition and stays live as the data changes. SORT returns a new block in the order you ask for and leaves the source alone. Typing inside a spilled block raises #SPILL!.

Nobody tells you which function to reach for. A sales summary, a lookup dashboard, a cleanup of an imported list and a budget against actuals each take two screens. The first builds the answer and the second reads it back off the sheet.

The audit gives you five sheets, each with one broken cell, and asks you to repair it from the error code. A division by an empty cell, a lookup with no matching row and text where a number belongs each need a different repair. Six exercises at level 3.
The capstones give you a business question and a workbook, with less scaffolding than the exercises before them.

Treat each one as a brief rather than a drill. Decide the shape of the answer first, write the formula second, and use the reading screen as the check that the first decision was right. The brief is the hard part and the formula is the easy part.

COUNT counts cells holding a number and passes over text, blanks and logical values. COUNTA counts anything that is not empty, so a date stored as text counts there and not here. COUNTIF adds one condition, and COUNTIFS adds as many as you like, provided each range covers the same rows. Wildcards go inside the quotes: a star for any run of characters, a question mark for exactly one.
Counting gets harder as soon as the column has gaps, text that looks like a number, or a condition attached.
Six exercises at levels 1 to 3, and the last one asks which count answers a given question.

The pair that trips people is COUNT and COUNTA on the same column. Run both on a list with three blanks and look at the gap, because that gap is the only reliable sign that some values are stored as text. Fixing the types changes the total, which is why the count comes first.
A date in Excel is a number with a format on it, and every date problem is a problem with that number.
DAYS subtracts one date from another. DATEDIF counts whole months or years between two dates, which is what an age column needs.
Five exercises at levels 2 and 3. The summary asks which distance between two dates a question needs.

TODAY and NOW recalculate whenever the file does. That suits one cell at the top of a report, and it costs time down a long column. DATE builds a date from a year, a month and a day, so you can construct a period instead of typing it.

Widen a date column and the number behind the format appears, usually in the forty-thousands. That is the check to make before any subtraction. A date typed as text will not subtract at all, and the error points at the formula rather than the cell.

#N/A means nothing matched, #VALUE! means a type is wrong, and #REF! means the reference no longer points at a cell. ISNA, ISERROR and ISERR test for them, and IFERROR catches every error and shows your own text. IFNA catches only the missing match, which is usually what people meant. A wide net hides a broken reference along with a missing code.
An error value is still a value, and this group is about reading one before deciding to hide it.
Four exercises at levels 2 and 3, and the summary asks which handler a given failure deserves.

The order matters more than the function. Read the code first, repair the cause where you can, and wrap only the failure you expect. A sheet of IFERROR wrappers is a sheet that no longer tells you when something breaks. Repair the cause first, then decide whether a wrapper earns its place at all.
INDEX and MATCH are two ordinary functions that combine into a lookup you can point in any direction.
Later exercises cover the two-way lookup, with MATCH on rows, MATCH on columns and INDEX at the intersection. Six exercises at levels 2 and 3.

MATCH returns the position of a value in a range, and INDEX returns the value at a row and column. Put those together and you can read left of the key column, which VLOOKUP cannot do. The two ranges are chosen separately, so no column count can drift. The group builds them one at a time so the combination arrives as a conclusion.

The zero in the third MATCH argument is the exact match, and leaving it out is the mistake that survives testing. A match type of one finds the nearest value below the key and returns a row that looks believable. Type the zero every time.

The first screen asks you to select A2 to A40 in one chord. Shift extends the selection, and Ctrl or Command turns the arrow key into a jump to the last filled cell. The jump stops at the first blank row, so a gap in the data ends the selection early. Press it, look at where the highlight stopped, and extend again from there.

The second screen keeps row 1 in view using the ribbon key tips: Alt, then W, then F, then R. A key tip is the letter each tab shows while Alt is held, so the route reads as a left-to-right walk across the ribbon. Freeze panes sits two levels in, and the same keys bring you back to unfreeze it.
This group has one exercise about moving around a sheet without the mouse.
Two screens, one at level 1, and no formula to type. The grader checks the range or the view you finish with, so a near miss is visible on the sheet rather than in a message.

A comparison such as B2>100 already returns TRUE or FALSE, so IF is often a wrapper around one. AND, OR and NOT combine tests without stacking IFs inside each other. IFS handles more than two outcomes, SWITCH matches a list of names, and the IS functions ask what a cell holds before you ask what it is worth.
IF turns a comparison into a decision, and this group builds the functions around it.
Seven exercises at levels 1 to 3. The pass-fail exercise is the shortest way to see the shape of the function, and the summary asks which one a question needs.

Two details carry most of the marks. The true and false results are evaluated left to right, so the first test that passes wins and the rest never run. Text returned by a test needs quotes around it and a number does not. Getting either wrong gives a result that looks right in one row and wrong in the next.
Looking a value up is routine work, and most of what goes wrong sits in the arguments people leave out.

Read every formula from the inside out: the value being matched, the block it is matched against, then the column it returns. Almost every wrong answer in this group is the third of those pointing somewhere plausible.
The last exercise puts VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP on one table and compares what each asks you to know. Ten exercises at levels 2 and 3, more than any other group.

VLOOKUP's fourth argument defaults to approximate match. A formula that works on sorted data can return a neighbour's number on unsorted data without an error. The group teaches both modes first, then HLOOKUP across rows, wildcards for partial keys, and a two-way lookup built from VLOOKUP and MATCH. XLOOKUP gets three exercises: exact match without counting columns, a search from the bottom, and a fallback that replaces IFERROR.

Each one combines functions from earlier groups: VLOOKUP against a tier table, SUMPRODUCT over paired ranges, MAX with a zero guard, IF and COUNTIF for a checklist. No new functions arrive. What changes is the size of the question, and one range that starts a row late still produces a plausible total. Checking the edges is most of the work.
Four exercises at level 3, each with two screens: build the sheet, then read a number back out of it.

The reading screen is the one to take slowly. A wrong total is often a right formula applied to a range that missed its last row, and a number read off the sheet will not say so. Recompute one line by hand and compare. Two screens also mean two chances to notice that a total is wrong.
This group is four small workbooks where the formulas have to agree with each other.

ROUND changes the value: 4450.3992 becomes 4450.4 in the cell, while a cell format only changes what you see. ROUNDUP and ROUNDDOWN move a price in one direction only. MROUND and FLOOR round to a multiple, so 47 can land on 45 or 50, and a pack of six ships 42 rather than a part-filled 48.
Rounding to two decimals on screen and rounding the stored number are different operations, and money cares about the difference.

The test worth running after each one is a sum of the rounded column against the rounded sum of the column. When the two totals disagree, a format is standing in for a calculation. That gap is exactly what a reconciliation at work looks for. Do it once on a price column and the habit sticks.
Three exercises, all at level 2. Each prompt names the rule and the unit, because nearest and up to the nearest produce different answers down a column.

A mean sent to a meeting that needed a median tells the room the wrong thing. The habit worth building is to look at the column before choosing the function, because one order ten times the usual size decides the answer. Each prompt in the group hides a distribution like that. Compare the two summaries on one column and the cost of the wrong choice shows.

AVERAGE can be dragged anywhere by one large value, and MEDIAN stays in the middle when it happens. MODE answers a different question: which value appears most often. LARGE and SMALL return the nth value from either end without sorting the list, and RANK turns a value into a position. MIN and MAX give the two ends of the column.
Seven exercises at levels 1 and 2, and the summary asks for the right number rather than the familiar one.
This group is about choosing which summary a column of numbers deserves.
Later exercises add several blocks in one call, build a running total with a locked starting row, and close with a summary asking which summing function a question needs.

Nine exercises run from level 1 to level 3, so the group starts at the smallest possible formula. Every prompt names the cell the total belongs in, and the answer is checked against the number the grader computed separately.

SUM skips text and blanks inside the range it is given. A number stored as text therefore disappears from a total with no warning, which is the failure the debugging exercise sets up. SUMIF takes the range to test first and the range to add second. SUMIFS reverses that order, and getting the two the wrong way round is the common mistake.
This group covers addition in a spreadsheet: one column, several blocks, and totals that include only the rows meeting a condition.
Four exercises at level 2. Each prompt shows the output you should see, so a tidy-up that changes a value is caught straight away.
Imported text arrives with its own casing, spacing and punctuation, and this group is the clean-up pass.

The ampersand and CONCAT join values and do not care what type they are. TEXTJOIN joins a whole range and can skip empty cells, which is the difference between a list and a list with gaps. UPPER, LOWER and PROPER normalise case, and PROPER is the one people forget until a mail merge prints names in capitals. SUBSTITUTE swaps every match, and a fourth argument picks one instance.

TRIM removes the spaces at the ends and collapses any run inside to one, which is what a pasted report needs. It does nothing for a non-breaking space, the character copied tables hide. When TRIM leaves a value looking unchanged, that space is the likely reason.
A lot of the text in a spreadsheet has to be measured or cut before it can be used.

LEN, LEFT and RIGHT give length and edges, enough to pull an order code apart. MID takes characters from the middle, and FIND and SEARCH locate a delimiter. FIND is case-sensitive, SEARCH is not, which decides whether a formula survives a typo, and wildcards in criteria find a name you only half remember. TEXTBEFORE and TEXTAFTER do the same split in one step.
Seven exercises at levels 1 to 3, and the summary asks which of these a task needs.

The hard part is the empty case. A delimiter that is missing returns an error from FIND, and LEFT built on that error fails too, so the fix is one test around the whole thing. Each exercise in the group has at least one row like that. Read one of them before you write the formula and the error handling writes itself.
